methods.title: Methods
methods.intro: How EarthTrend Detective turns raw NASA records into a trend verdict — plain language first, numbers behind it.
methods.teaser: Every result here comes from the same NASA data and the same two statistical tests, explained in full on the

dataSource.title: 01. NASA Data
dataSource.body: Every case uses NASA POWER's MERRA-2 reanalysis (temporal/monthly/point), a ~50 km-resolution model of the atmosphere and land surface built from satellite and ground observations — not a single weather station.

aggregation.title: 02. Building the Series
aggregation.body: Monthly values are filtered for missing readings (coded -999) and aggregated into annual or seasonal totals/averages, matching each variable's unit rule: temperature is a mean, precipitation is summed, soil wetness is a mean.

tests.title: 03. The Statistical Tests
tests.body: Mann-Kendall checks whether a trend is unlikely to be random noise and returns a p-value. Sen's Slope estimates how much change per year or decade, even when the data is noisy.

limitations.title: 04. Limitations
limitations.body: A statistically significant trend shows a real, unlikely-by-chance change — it does not, by itself, prove a single cause. MERRA-2 describes a ~50 km grid cell, not an exact point, and year-to-year values can be correlated with each other (autocorrelation); both are flagged as warnings when they apply.
limitations.context: Comparing a Rondônia case to an Arctic one shows how differently climate change plays out by region — useful for classroom environmental education and for reading land-cover data like MapBiomas alongside it. This tool supports conversations around UN Sustainable Development Goals 6 (Clean Water), 13 (Climate Action), and 15 (Life on Land) — it doesn't replace them.
